newsitem.title: UK: Racal moves to deliver overdue turnaround.
newsitem.headline: Racal moves to deliver overdue turnaround.

text.p: Racal Electronics Plc is like the man on death row who has just won a temporary reprieve.

After two profit warnings since December and a shareprice slump in what was supposed to be its turnaround year, Racal vowed to investors at its results a month ago that this time it would deliver a recovery.
Investors gave Racal a temporary stay of execution, but analysts have warned that failure to deliver this time round will ensure there is no mercy from big shareholders.
On June 3 Racal launched a strategic revamp based on refocusing the group on its three core activities: telecommunications, data products and defence electronics.
David Elsbury, chief executive, pacified angry shareholders by launching a charm offensive in the weeks afterwards to persuade them to give Racal another chance.
Since then shares have steadied and are now trading at 243 pence per share, up from the year low of 213, but still well below 345 pence a year ago.

Reflecting on the failures of the group over the past year, Elsbury admitted in an interview "It was the most regrettable things in my 41 years (at the company) to have two profit warnings in four months.
"It damaged morale. It hurt. I lost a lot of money. But I intend to get that money back."

The shareholder reprieve has injected a new lease of life into the group which has implemented a series of reviews and cost-cutting initiatives -- including 1,000 job cuts -- to increase shareholder value.
In an interview at Racal's defence electronics base in Bracknell in south-east England, Elsbury outlined why investors should believe that Racal can deliver this time after failing in the past.
First among Racal's options is the idea for a partial U.S. flotation of the troubled data products division which triggered the April 18 profit warning.

"We have appointed Goldman Sachs as advisers to see whether flotation is the right way forward," he told Reuters. "We can't float less than 20 percent (under U.S. regulations). We have four options in all: keep it, close as we will never be able to get it right, partially float it or form a joint venture."
The final decision will be taken by the Racal board by March next year, said Elsbury.

The second option would be to find a partner for its telecoms business, something which Racal is already discussing with a number of potential partners. The division is one of the largest data network providers serving blue-chip companies and has the second biggest British telecoms network after British Telecommunications Plc.

Elsbury said the interested parties included global players looking for an entry into Britain, country-bound companies looking to expand internationally, British start-up telecoms players and information providers.
Racal is looking for a provider which gives it a global delivery system for its international traffic.
The telecoms business is Racal's fastest growing. It currently has a quarter of group revenues at 281 million pounds and that it seen growing to 500 million by 2001..
"That figure of 500 million would give us growth of 15 percent a year, without a partnership deal. With a partner we see telecoms growing at 25 percent a year," said Elsbury.

On the defence front, Elsbury says he is convinced Racal will be able to retain its independence as European rationalisation looks like slipping further down the line with the continued uncertainty over the future of French defence-electronics firm Thomson-CSF.
Though earlier on Friday, French prime minister Lionel Jospin said the government was "flexible" on privatisation, fuelling rumours that Thomson-CSF's future could be in the frame again.

Elsbury had told a press briefing in Bracknell this week "I think the need for Racal to marry someone bigger has been pushed back. Which is good for us. This independence allows us to work with all the key players -- Lockheed Martin, GEC, British Aerospace and Thomson."

One boost for the defence division in recent months was the decision last December for Racal's Yeoman consortium to merge with its rival bidder for the two billion pounds Bowman defence communications contract, guaranteeing it a share of the deal.

The new combined consortium, called Archer, has halved its development costs as a result. Elsbury said it expected Archer to get 70 percent of the related export market, with the main competitor being Thomson-CSF.
"Worldwide exports should exceed two billion (for Archer)," he said. --London newsroom +44 171 542 4043
